asks: How is a fork made on each system?
answer: On every system, a fork starts from a copy-on-write copy of its parent's disk, or of one of its checkpoints: an APFS clone on a Mac, a reflink copy on a Linux host, for macOS and Linux computers alike (`work-on-top-of-libkrun`, `fork-shares-disk-blocks`). It then boots cold, so a program that ran in its parent runs in the fork only when something starts it. A Linux fork boots cold until libkrun can save a computer's memory (`forks-of-running-linux`). A macOS fork always boots cold, since Apple's framework cannot move a saved memory state to a new identity.
